translation: Two other small, scallop-edged photos, likely from the same year, show the same little girl looking even smaller in a dress with flounces and puff sleeves.
In the first photo, she nestles cheekily against a woman with a hefty physique encased in a wide-striped dress; her hair styled into thick rolls.
In the second photo, she raises her left fist while her right one is held by a tall man wearing light-colored jacket and pleated pants with nonchalant posture.
Both pictures were taken on the same day in front of low brick wall topped by boundary of flowers in cobbled courtyard.
Above their heads stretches hanging line where an errant pin remains secured.

Another photo, also signed by the same photographer but with more ordinary paper and the gold border gone probably destined for the same family distribution shows a little girl about four years old, serious, almost sad despite her plump healthy face beneath short hair, parted in the middle and pulled back by barrettes to which ribbons are attached like butterflies.
Her left hand rests on the same carved table in view here, Louis XVI style.
She appears pudgy in her blouse; her suspender skirt rises at the front due to a protruding belly that might indicate rickets (around 1944).
The boys were proud to join the regiment and they were considered handsome in their uniforms.
On the night of their military fitness examination, they would tour the cafes to celebrate the glory of being recognized as real men.
Before joining the regiment, they were still seen as kids and had little value on the job market or for marriage.
Afterwards, they could have a wife and children.
The uniforms that they wore around their neighbourhood while on leave wrapped them in a cloak of patriotic beauty and implied sacrifice.
The shadow of victorious fighters, like GIs, hovered around them.
The coarse cloth of their uniform jackets brushed against when one stood on tiptoe to kiss them, materialized an absolute divide between men and women's world.
Seeing these young soldiers evoked a feeling of heroism.

Beneath their unchanging appearance, last year's circus posters featuring a picture of Roger Lanzac, and first communion pictures distributed among friends, the "Club des Chansonniers" on Radio Luxembourg filled their days with new desires.
On Sunday afternoons, they would crowd around the storefront window of the general electronics store to watch television.
Cafes invested in buying a set to attract customers.
Motocross trails snaked up and down hill sides and all day people watched as machines deafeningly ascended and descended.
The growing restlessness of commerce with its new buzzwords "initiative", "dynamism" were shaking up towns' daily routines.
Between fairgrounds and village festivals, 'Commercial Fortnight' became a springtime ritual.
Downtown speakers blared encouragements to buy interspersed with songs from Annie Cordy and Eddie Constantine; prizes ranging from winning a Simca or an entire dining room set were announced.
On stage was a local presenter at Town Hall Square making everyone laugh at jokes by Roger Nicolas and Jean Richard while cajoling volunteers for Quitte ou Double just like on the radio shows.

Sitting modestly off to one side under her crown sat the Commercial Queen presiding over it all; merchandise progressed underneath festive colors attracting multitudes who remarked "It's so different" or "we shouldn't hold back we're dulling our minds staying at home.
But they only talked about what they had seen, which could be relived by eating and drinking.
They didn't have the talent or conviction to discuss what they knew but hadn't witnessed.
Therefore, there were no talk of Jewish children boarding trains for Auschwitz, nor of the starving dead collected in the morning in the Warsaw Ghetto, nor about 10,000 degrees at Hiroshima.

Hence this impression that history lessons, documentaries and movies later wouldn't dissipate: neither crematorium ovens nor atomic bombs fell into the same era as black-market butter, air raid warnings and basement shelters.
They started to make comparisons with the previous war, the Great War of 14, which was won in blood and glory, a war of men that the women at the table listened to with respect.
They talked about Chemin des Dames and Verdun, about gas attacks and bells ringing on November 11th, 1918.
They mentioned villages from which not a single child who'd gone to war had returned.
They contrasted soldiers stuck in muddy trenches with those taken prisoner in '40 who were safe and warm for five years without even bombs falling on their heads.
They argued over heroism and misfortune.

The children did not listen and were quick to leave the table as soon as they had been given permission, taking advantage of the general goodwill on festive days to get up to forbidden games, jumping on beds and swinging upside down.
But everything registered.

Beside the fabled era, whose episodes they would not organize for a long time the Debacle, Exodus, Occupation, Landing and Victory they found the nameless time in which they were growing up rather dull.
They regretted not having been born or being barely alive when they needed to take part in mass exoduses onto roads and sleep on straw like gypsies.
They would forever lament this unlived period; others' memories instilled in them a secret nostalgia for this era that they had narrowly missed but hoped one day to experience.
The frenzy that had followed the Liberation was fading.
People then only thought of going out and the world was full of desires to be satisfied immediately.
Everything that constituted a first since the war triggered a rush, bananas, national Lottery tickets, fireworks.

In whole neighborhoods, from the grandmother supported by her daughters to the infant in a pram, people rushed to the funfair, torchlight processions or Bouglione's circus where they almost got trampled in the commotion.
They gathered as pleading and singing crowds on roads welcoming Notre-Dame de Boulogne's statue and escorting it kilometers further on next day.
Secular or religious, all opportunities were good for them to be outside together as if they wished to continue living collectively.
On Sunday evenings, buses came back from sea with tall young men in shorts singing at top of their lungs while perched on luggage racks atop vehicles.
Dogs roamed freely mating in middle of streets.
Family narrative and social narrative were one and the same.
The voices of the diners defined the spaces of their youth: the countryside and farms where, in time lost to memory, men had been groomers and women servants;
factories where everyone had met, socialized, and married;
small-scale trades where those who were most ambitious had made their foray.

They outlined stories devoid of personal events other than births, weddings, and deaths, without travel except perhaps for army services in some far-off garrison town lives filled with hard labor, its wear-and-tear grind-downs bested only by threats presented by boozing.
School was a mythical backdrop a brief golden age presided over by a strict schoolmaster with his iron ruler ready to rap errant knuckles.
Browned photos, their backs stained by all the fingers that had held them at other meals, a mix of coffee and melted grease forming an indefinable color, passed from hand to hand.
In the stiff and serious newlyweds, the wedding guests arrayed in several rows along a wall, one could recognize neither parents nor anyone else.
One did not see oneself either in the partially naked baby of indistinct sex on a cushion but someone else, a creature belonging to a silent and inaccessible time.
